\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Randomised experiments on a social or marketplace network violate the assumption that one unit's outcome does not depend on another's assignment, and the quantity of interest is usually the \emph{global average treatment effect} (GATE): the difference in mean outcome if every unit were treated rather than none.
Difference in means (DM) is biased for it; design-based estimators with an exposure mapping \citep{aronow2017estimating,ugander2013graph,eckles2017design} are unbiased only if the mapping is right, and weight the few units whose exposure is extreme.
\emph{Regression adjustment} \citep{chin2019regression,han2023model} avoids both: fit the outcome on the unit's own treatment and graph-based exposure covariates such as the treated fraction of its neighbours, then predict at the all-treated and all-control assignments and difference the predictions. It uses every unit and needs no weights.

How well it works, what governs its error and when it fails is not known.
The estimator fits a model where exposures occur and evaluates it where they do not: under Bernoulli($p$) assignment a unit with $d$ neighbours sees a treated fraction concentrated around $p$ with spread $\sqrt{p(1-p)/d}$, and the two global corners, fraction $1$ and fraction $0$, lie far outside it.
\citet{chin2019regression} points this out qualitatively and draws the analogy to off-policy evaluation.
We take it as the organising idea, not as a novelty, and ask what it predicts and whether the predictions hold.
Our reading is that the error has two parts with different drivers: the \emph{variance} is the leverage of the corner contrast in the regression, which grows with degree; the \emph{bias} is the response's curvature times the raw distance from the observed exposures to the corner, which does not grow with degree for a smooth response and which no regression can estimate from data that never visit the corner.

We test this on simulated experiments in which the GATE is known exactly, so that each estimator's error, bias and variance are measured. The simulations cross six interference mechanisms, five synthetic graph families and two real Facebook graphs, Bernoulli and graph-cluster assignment, and DM, H\'ajek estimators, the regression and its richer specifications, oracle forms and data-adaptive learners. The predictions and the acceptance rule for a diagnostic were written down before the runs.

\paragraph{What we find.}

shown.message:
I updated the paper with the numbers `experiment-repo` confirmed. I also found and fixed a page-limit overflow. The updated paper is on `dev` (1a26df3) and on the candidate branch behind paper-repo#9.

- **Overflow:** the main text had been running two lines past nine pages since the last Fig 7 change, and my additions pushed it about ten lines over. I moved detail to the appendix and cut some wording. A local build now ends the main text on page 9 with the References heading on page 10, but page 9 is full to the last line, so the layout is still tight.
- **Number changes in the text:**
  - The 0.55 slope is now accounted for by the realised leverage exponents: 1.09 in 1+d, −0.02 in n and −0.99 in p(1−p).
  - The decision-rule accuracies now carry intervals. Rule B is 91.8% [89.3, 93.8], and always using regression is 80.2% [74.7, 85.4]. The rule adds 12 points [7, 16].
  - The cluster-design result at d=20 now quotes the 68/78, 62/78 and 54/78 comparisons.
  - The noise-adjusted S result now gives its own R² of −0.005 on 1283 cells, and −0.064 only on the 1215-cell subset.
- **Definitions corrected:**
  - Bias, SD and RMSE are pooled over the draws of a cell, and SD includes the variation between graph draws.
  - The signal-to-noise ratio is measured net of the unit baseline.
  - The data splits used for the diagnostic are now described as they were run.
  - "Win" means the point estimate in the decision rule and the interval in the regime shares.
- **Hedged:** the explanation for the non-monotone bias of the threshold mechanism (d) is now worded as only partly supported.
- **Moved to the appendix:** the predicted break-even spillover share, the cluster-bootstrap coverage (83% of 396 cluster cells) and the acceptance-rule criteria.
- **Not done:** the fine-p result for the saturating mechanism (c) is still pending, so the text keeps the five-point-grid statement. `experiment-repo` has also not yet confirmed the appendix Grid paragraph.

I replied on paper-repo#4 with these points. paper-repo#9 now waits on its remaining reviews and checks, and I'll update the coverage and (c) text when `experiment-repo` delivers its next aggregation.
